title: The Dilemma of Difference (Part 1): SEND as a Wicked Problem
author: Matthew Evans
summary: Matthew Evans opens what he frames as a possible series on special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) by proposing a framing device rather than a solution: treat SEND as a 'wicked problem' in the Rittel and Webber sense -- resistant to resolution, not evil, and prone to 'metamorphism,' where prior attempts to solve it reshape how it re-emerges. He grounds this in Seymour Sarason's 'lock-step problem' -- the tension built into mass schooling between individual differences and a graded, age-cohort system -- and Brahm Norwich's 'dilemma of difference,' the underlying question of whether recognizing difference helps or harms. Evans traces how EHCP demand, parental advocacy, and resource scarcity have interacted to produce the current SEND crisis in England, arguing this isn't a case of one bad policy but a self-reinforcing pattern created by earlier well-intentioned fixes. He closes with eight 'rules of engagement' for entering the debate with humility rather than certainty, deliberately avoiding a call to return to a prior system (Statements) or import a model from elsewhere, since complex systems can't simply be reversed.
points: Evans's central framing device -- SEND as a 'wicked problem' with 'metamorphism' -- explains why repeated policy fixes keep producing new versions of the same underlying tension rather than resolving it.

Sarason's 'lock-step problem' (a graded school system assumes rough uniformity of pace among same-age children, which reality constantly contradicts) is presented as the structural root that adaptive teaching, differentiation, and EHCPs are all attempts to patch.

His case study of self-reinforcing dysfunction: giving parents more voice to pursue an EHCP, combined with resources being statutorily pulled toward EHCP-holders, increases the incentive to seek a diagnosis, which increases EHCP demand further.

Evans's eight rules of engagement (seek to open debate, ask what people mean by contested terms like 'inclusion,' resist tame solutions, accept no full resolution) are offered as a discipline for entering a polarized debate without either false certainty or paralysis.
quotes: I don't know anywhere near enough about the topic of SEND. Second, I hold my ideas on this very lightly.

What crisis? Well, let's start with the rapidly accelerating number of children with EHCPs in England, the local authorities on the verge of bankruptcy, the shortfall of places in specialist settings, the litigation, the conflict between parents and institutions.

A graded school system, taking a new crop of children every year at five or six years of age, moving them through their studies in ‘lock-step’ fashion ‘til graduation, makes an assumption about the equality, motivation, and performance for children of similar age that the reality of individual differences rudely challenges.
Metamorphism describes the way that some problems re-emerge over time, despite our attempts to solve them (like whack-a-mole).

As EHCP numbers increase resources are pulled towards those pupils who have an EHCP (as it is a statutory requirement to meet need), fewer resources are available to meet the need of pupils without an EHCP, therefore increasing the incentive to get one.
Neither can we transplant a system from another jurisdiction. We should certainly look at what happens in other countries and learn from this, but context is everything.
